extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social psychology, sociology, political theory, and law; informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies criteria used to classify, explain, and predict crowd behaviour (heterogeneous vs homogeneous, anonymous vs non-anonymous, criminal crowds, juries), and the effects of crowds on politics, the press, and legal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemeral nature of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions are now ephemeral: the extreme mobility of ideas and the newspaper press expose crowds to continually contrary opinions so that no opinion succeeds in becoming widespread; "An opinion nowadays dies out before it has found a sufficiently wide acceptance to become general."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why sustained public opinion is rare in the modern press-driven age; provides cause (newspapers, mobility of ideas) and consequence (governments cannot form stable policies based on durable public beliefs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerlessness of governments to direct opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments no longer direct opinion; instead they follow it, often adopting unstable conduct out of dread or terror of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate the relation between authorities and crowds: when crowd power increases and is unchecked, statesmen aim to follow rather than lead public sentiment; examples include alliances (Franco-Russian) shaped by popular movements and leaders consenting to interviews to submit views to crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as reflection rather than director of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The press has become chiefly the reflection of the opinions of crowds and their incessant variations; it has renounced enforcing an idea or doctrine and confines itself to supplying information under competitive pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how commercial pressures and competition cause newspapers to follow public taste (news, gossip, puffs), suppress sustained criticism, and thereby hasten the transience of opinions; cites French papers and the decline of literary/theatrical criticism as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics governed by sentiment rather than reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Political life is increasingly swayed by the impulses of changeable crowds who are uninfluenced by reason and guided by sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess political phenomena where emotional crowd responses (sentiment) dominate rational deliberation; supports reading of political events as emotionally driven rather than analytically argued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence and indifference of modern convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The destruction of general beliefs leads to extreme divergence of convictions and a growing indifference among crowds to anything not directly touching their immediate interests; doctrines recruit only among the quite illiterate or very committed classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains social fragmentation: working classes may hold strong doctrine-based views, while lower middle classes tend toward scepticism or instability; useful for predicting which social strata will sustain ideological movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of tyrannical dominance if a single opinion gains prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single opinion were to acquire sufficient prestige it would enforce general acceptance and become tyrannical, closing the era of free discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a cautionary criterion: evaluates potential dangers when an opinion becomes dominant within powerful crowds given their capriciousness and potential for despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental role of race in shaping crowd character
rubrics_metrics.description: Race (the genius of the race) is the most powerful factor determining a crowd's dispositions—crowds composed of a single race differ markedly from mixed-race crowds; the stronger the spirit of the race, the less pronounced the inferior characteristics of crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a classificatory and explanatory principle: compare Latin, English, French crowds for tendencies (centralisation/dictatorship vs private initiative vs emphasis on equality/liberty); used to predict cultural differences in crowd behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: heterogeneous vs homogeneous crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are classified into heterogeneous crowds (individuals of any description) and homogeneous crowds (sects, castes, classes), with heterogeneous ones further divided into anonymous (street crowds) and non-anonymous (juries, assemblies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structural rubric for analysis: identify the crowd's type to anticipate characteristic behaviours (e.g., anonymity reduces responsibility; homogeneous crowds have different bonding mechanisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous vs non-anonymous crowds: responsibility differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous crowds (e.g., street crowds) lack the sentiment of responsibility present in non-anonymous crowds (e.g., juries, assemblies), leading to different tendencies in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing crowd actions, check anonymity: anonymous settings foster less responsibility and potentially more impulsive acts; non-anonymous settings may restrain some impulses owing to accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneous crowds: intelligence has little influence
rubrics_metrics.description: In heterogeneous crowds intelligence is without influence: collectivities act under the sway of unconscious sentiments and suggestion rather than individual intellectual capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why assemblies of specialists do not necessarily deliver more reasoned judgments than lay crowds; practical implication: efforts to 'improve' a crowd by selecting more intelligent members may fail to change its decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd traits: openness to suggestion, credulity, mobility, exaggeration of sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are characterised by openness to suggestion, credulity, extreme mobility of ideas, and the exaggeration of sentiments (good or bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic diagnostic features to identify crowd psychology at work; used to explain rapid shifts in collective behaviour and the susceptibility of crowds to persuasive influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal crowds: automatic, unconscious obedience to suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal crowds often enter a purely automatic and unconscious state guided by suggestion; participants believe they are performing patriotic duty rather than criminal acts (illustrated by the Bastille murder and September massacres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames mass violence as psychological process rather than individual criminal intent; examples show how ordinary people can commit atrocious acts under collective suggestion and approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary crowd morality and ad hoc judicial forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds manifest rudimentary conceptions of justice and morality—forming improvised tribunals, judging by appearance/reputation, alternating ferocity and tenderness, and devising crude 'procedures' (e.g., forcing victims to pass between slaughterers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to interpret crowd-imposed justice as internally coherent to the crowd's mentality, not as legitimate law; exemplified by improvised trials during massacres and the selective nature of who is deemed guilty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juries as a distinct category: heterogeneous but not anonymous
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries exemplify heterogeneous crowds that are not anonymous; they display suggestibility and limited reasoning capacity but are influenced by leaders and unconscious sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing legal decision-making, treat juries as crowd phenomena—expect sentimental influences, leader effects, and resistance to purely technical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdicts independent of jury composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical observations show that jury verdicts remain essentially the same regardless of the social or educational composition of juries; selecting enlightened jurors historically did not alter outcomes ('ITS VERDICTS HAVE REMAINED THE SAME').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges reforms premised on changing juror makeup to produce different verdicts; suggests causes lie in crowd psychology rather than individual juror qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juries are more susceptible to sentiment than to argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries are strongly impressed by sentimental considerations (e.g., a mother breastfeeding, orphans, agreeable appearance) and only slightly moved by logical argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal advocacy should prioritise emotional appeals and evocative presentation over extended technical reasoning when addressing juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential leniency: juries indulgent to passion, severe to personally dangerous crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries tend to be lenient toward crimes motivated by passion (infanticide, revenge against seducers) and severe toward crimes that pose direct danger to jurors themselves; juries instinctively divide crimes into those dangerous or not to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predict sentencing tendencies: appeals based on passion motives may find jury sympathy; crimes perceived as socially dangerous provoke harsher juror responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige and distinction bias in juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries are profoundly influenced by prestige: name, birth, great wealth, celebrity, and the assistance of an illustrious counsel all benefit the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for prestige effects when assessing trial outcomes or fairness; prominent characteristics of the accused can tilt juror sentiment regardless of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratorical tactic: identify and sway leading jurors rather than all jurors
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective counsel observes jurors, identifies the two or three influential members, secures their adhesion, then converts the rest; prepared speeches have little effect—pleadings must adapt to juror reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advocacy guideline: dynamic, situational rhetoric and personal rapport with key jurors are more effective than static argumentation; anecdote of Lachaud and the 'seventh juryman' illustrates small changes (pleasing or accommodating a juror) can win them over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd leadership effect: a small minority directs the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: In crowds and juries, a small number of energetic individuals serve as guides whose opinions carry the rest; persuading these leaders suffices to determine the crowd's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic and tactical implication: interventions should target opinion-leaders within the group to achieve broader consensus; counsel should focus on these individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury as institutional check on magistrates and abstract law
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury tempers the severity of law-bound judges, providing social pity and mitigating rigid, technical application of law; abolishing juries risks replacing a variable, humane check with an unforgiving professional magistracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative argument for maintaining juries: they can correct magistrates' errors and avoid mechanically applying punishment without consideration of individual circumstances.
